newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bonds rally, but U.S. test ahead.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bonds rally, but U.S. test ahead.

text.p: *Australian bonds rallied after a much weaker than expected labour force report, but the long end proved more restrained ahead of two sets of key U.S. data over the next two days.
*Market outperforms the bloc apart from N.Z. short end.
By Colin Brinsden

Australian bonds rallied after a much weaker than expected labour force report, but the market did not get too carried away with the news and the long end in particular remains wary of upcoming events in the U.S.

The data follows a run of indicators pointing to an accelerating economy, and was generally viewed by economists as not having any implications for monetary policy and that the Reserve Bank would retain its "on hold" stance for some time.
Indeed, housing finance for January released at the same time saw a further 5.0 percent rise in growth.

Matthew Drennan, senior economist at Axiom Funds Management, said the market faces the prospect of accelerating activity in a number of key sectors such as housing construction, a worsening current account deficit, the threat of modest wage inflation and slippage in the fiscal position.
"On balance, not what you would describe as a favouable environment," Drennan added.

However, the labour force report lifted the market from an initial weak performance. Employment fell 7,200, when a 10,000 rise had been expected, and reflected a large 24,200 drop in full-time employment.
The unemployment rate also rose to 8.8 percent when it had been expected to remain at 8.6 percent.

Late on Wednesday and before the data, Prime Minister John Howard had conceded that the economy needed to grow at 4.0 to 4.5 percent to substantially cut unemployment, well above its long-term trend rate of near 3.0 percent growth.
However, his Employment Minister Amanda Vanstone said the government was on track to meet its budget forecasts for unemployment and employment for 1996/97.
The data saw the 10-year yield spread to the U.S. narrow to around 120 basis points, its lowest since end-February.
However, Su-Lin Ong, fixed income economist at Hambros Bank, still holds a medium term view that this spread will blow out again over the coming months.
"As signs of a strengthening economy continue to emerge in the coming months, the spread is likely to widen to around 150 basis points in six months," Ong said.

The focus now switches to the U.S., which faces retail sales for February later today and its PPI for the same month on Friday. The market there is already under cloud on the possibility of a tightening in policy when the Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25.
